title: New Integrated Shield Plan rider rules: premiums, co-payments and insurer oversight
asked: Four MPs asked about the new Integrated Shield Plan rider requirements: whether there will be a cap on patients' out-of-pocket costs, how families facing large co-payments will be supported, whether insurers can keep older higher-coverage policies, what safeguards stop insurers from reducing coverage for ageing policyholders, and how MOH and MAS regulate insurers.
asked_by: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Ms Poh Li San, Dr Hamid Razak and Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
response: Mr Ong Ye Kung answered the four questions together. He said patient load has been shifting from private to public hospitals for 15 years, from 15:85 in 2010 to 10:90 now, with private hospital IP premiums rising about 17% a year and about 100,000 policyholders cancelling or downgrading riders annually. The new rider requirements apply only to riders bought on or after 27 November 2025; premiums should be about 30% lower, riders will not cover the minimum deductible and will require higher co-payment, with a 5% co-payment cap of $6,000 a year on top of deductibles. He projected six in 10 claimants would pay no cash after MediSave, most of the rest $1,000 or less, and said MOH and MAS work closely together on oversight while the Government does not regulate private insurers' premiums.

key_points.point: Patient load has shifted from private to public hospitals over 15 years, from 15:85 in 2010 to 10:90 now.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: In 2010, the split between private and public was 15:85.

key_points.point: Private hospital IP premiums grew about 17% a year over the past three years.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: IP premiums for private hospital have been growing at an average rate of 17% annually for the past three years

key_points.point: About 100,000 policyholders cancel or downgrade their IP rider policies each year.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: every year, about 100,000 policyholders cancel or downgrade their IP rider policies

key_points.point: The new requirements apply only to riders purchased on or after 27 November 2025; insurers decide their approach for earlier policies.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: the new requirements for IP riders will only affect policyholders who purchased riders on or after 27 November 2025

key_points.point: Premiums under the new rider design should be about 30% lower than existing maximum-coverage policies.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: IP rider premiums under the new design should be lower, on average 30% lower, compared to existing policies with maximum coverage

key_points.point: New riders will not cover the minimum IP deductible and will require higher co-payment.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: the new IP rider policies will not cover the minimum IP deductibles and also require higher co-payment

key_points.point: Co-payment is capped at 5% up to $6,000 a year, on top of deductibles.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: there will still be a cap of 5% co-payment up to $6,000 a year, in addition to the deductibles

key_points.point: MOH projects six in 10 rider claimants will not pay cash out-of-pocket after MediSave.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: We project that six in 10 rider claimants should not have to pay cash out-of-pocket after MediSave.

key_points.point: A 60-year-old on a maximum-coverage private hospital IP and rider can save about $1,600 a year in premiums by switching to the new rider.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: A 60-year-old on a private hospital IP and rider with maximum coverage, can now save about $1,600 a year in premiums by switching to the new rider.

key_points.point: On support for families, patients should weigh financial and healthcare needs and can seek subsidised care in public hospitals if affordability is an issue.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: Patients should consider their financial and healthcare needs when choosing where to seek care, including seeking subsidised care in public hospitals should affordability become an issue.

key_points.point: Public health capacity is being expanded, and surge capacity for selected treatments may be used if needed.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: If need be, we may need to implement surge capacity for selected treatments.

key_points.point: MOH and MAS work closely together on regulatory oversight of IP insurers.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: MOH’s key role is to oversee the development and operation of the public healthcare system and ensure universal access to healthcare.

key_points.point: MOH intervenes in the market only when a serious market failure emerges.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: We only step in when we see a serious market failure emerging

key_points.point: Private insurers' premiums are not regulated by the Government.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: The Government does not regulate their premiums.

key_points.point: Policyholders who give up their riders can fall back on public subsidised healthcare.
key_points.speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
key_points.quote: there is always public subsidised healthcare

left_open: Whether MOH will set a loss-ratio efficiency requirement for private insurers
Whether the 5% co-payment cap of $6,000 a year also caps total out-of-pocket costs including deductibles
What safeguards apply to policyholders who bought riders before 27 November 2025, beyond individual insurers' own decisions
supplementary: Safeguards for existing and older policyholders, adverse selection, insurer premium hikes, and public hospital capacity and wait times.
